summary.text: The triple point of a substance is the single temperature and pressure at which its solid, liquid and gas phases can all coexist in equilibrium.
On a phase diagram it is where the sublimation, fusion and vaporisation curves meet; for water it lies at 273.16 K and a vapor pressure of about 611.657 pascals.
Triple-point cells give highly precise, repeatable temperatures, so they are used to calibrate thermometers and to anchor the ITS-90 temperature scale.

facts.label: Old SI role
facts.value: Water's triple point defined the kelvin until 2019

items.prompt: A chunk of ice floats in the near-vacuum of outer space, at a pressure far below water's triple point, and is warmed. What happens to it?

options.label: It melts into liquid water, then boils away
It turns straight into vapor without becoming liquid
It stays solid no matter how much it is warmed
It shatters into smaller pieces of ice

items.explain: Below the triple point pressure liquid water cannot exist, so ice sublimates directly into vapor when heated.

items.prompt: A lab wants a thermometer checked against a temperature that can be reproduced exactly every time. What makes a sealed cell of pure water suitable?

options.label: Water boils at the same temperature everywhere on Earth
Pure water never freezes, so it stays steady
Ice, water and vapor coexist only at one fixed point
Water's temperature is set by the lab's air pressure

items.explain: Solid, liquid and gas coexist only at the triple point, which gives a highly precise, reproducible temperature.

items.prompt: On a phase diagram, three curves, for sublimation, fusion and vaporisation, all meet at one spot. What is that spot called?

options.label: The triple point
The critical point
The Curie point
The lambda point

items.explain: The triple point is where the sublimation, fusion and vaporisation curves meet.

items.prompt: For most substances, liquid cannot exist below the temperature of the gas-liquid-solid triple point, but water is an exception. What is different about water?

options.label: Water has no solid phase at ordinary pressures
Water vapor turns directly into liquid at any cold temperature
Water's triple point lies at a much higher pressure
The melting point of ordinary ice falls as pressure rises

items.explain: Because ice's melting point decreases with pressure, liquid water can exist below the triple point temperature when compressed.

items.prompt: Triple-point cells for water use a set isotope mix rather than any natural sample. Why?

options.label: Different isotope mixes shift the triple point slightly
Natural isotopes make the water freeze too quickly
A set mix keeps the water from becoming a gas
Isotopes of water change the pressure of the room

items.explain: Variations in isotopic composition cause small changes in the triple point, so a specific composition is used.

items.prompt: Today the kelvin is fixed through the Boltzmann constant. What does that make water's triple point?

options.label: Still the exact definition of one kelvin
A measured value that matters but no longer defines the unit
A temperature that no longer has any use
A value that is now defined as 273 K exactly

items.explain: After the 2019 revision the triple point of water is no longer a defining point, though its empirical value remains important.
